[Figure 1]

To understand how the intensity of tariff rhetoric in trade-policy announcements affects public reception, policy researchers Elena Vasquez-Torres and Frances Johansson measured study participants' responses to three versions of the same trade-policy announcement—a control version using neutral tone, a version using highly intense tariff rhetoric, and a version using mildly intense tariff rhetoric. Reviewing the data, a student concludes that the mere presence of tariff rhetoric in an announcement may not negatively affect readers' perceptions of the announcement's clarity, but highly intense tariff rhetoric in an announcement does worsen readers' perceptions of the announcement's clarity.
prompt: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student's conclusion?

choices.A: On average, participants' ratings of the clarity of the announcement were substantially higher than were participants' ratings of the trading partner regardless of which type of announcement participants had seen.
choices.B: Compared with participants who saw the control announcement, participants who saw the low-intensity announcement rated the announcement as slightly more clear, whereas participants who saw the high-intensity announcement rated the announcement as less clear.
choices.C: Participants who saw the low-intensity announcement rated the announcement as slightly more clear than participants who saw the control announcement did, but participants' attitude toward the trading partner was slightly worse when participants saw the low-intensity announcement than when they saw the neutral announcement.
choices.D: Compared with participants who saw the low-intensity announcement, participants who saw the high-intensity announcement rated the announcement as less clear and had a less positive attitude toward the trading partner.

explanation:
Choice B is the best answer. The student's conclusion is that mildly intense tariff rhetoric does not negatively affect readers' perceptions of the announcement's clarity, whereas highly intense tariff rhetoric does negatively affect those perceptions. This choice accurately describes the supporting data from the 'clarity of announcement' portion of the graph: participants who saw the low-intensity announcement rated it as slightly more clear than those who saw the control announcement, while participants who saw the high-intensity announcement rated it as less clear than those who saw the control announcement.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect. This choice does not support the student's conclusion. The conclusion is only about how participants perceive the clarity of the announcement; participants' attitude toward the trading partner is not relevant to the claim.
